item.title: AIDS 2026 Conference ends with scientific hope, funding uncertainty
item.description:
The world's largest HIV conference concluded in Rio de Janeiro on Friday with a clear message: while scientific advances have brought humanity closer than ever to ending AIDS, declining global funding now poses the greatest threat to achieving that goal.
After six days of scientific presentations, policy debates and community discussions, delegates at the 26th International AIDS Conference (AIDS 2026) celebrated major advances in HIV prevention and treatment while warning that shrinking financial support could reverse decades of progress.
More than 7,000 researchers, policymakers, health professionals, activists and people living with HIV from over 175 countries attended the conference under the theme "Rethink. Rebuild. Rise."
The overriding conclusion was that science is no longer the biggest barrier to ending HIV; equitable access is.
Researchers presented promising data on long-acting HIV prevention medicines, simplified treatment strategies and next-generation therapies that could dramatically reduce new infections and improve treatment adherence. Experts described the findings as the most significant advances since antiretroviral therapy transformed HIV from a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition.
Delegates, however, cautioned that these breakthroughs will have limited impact unless governments, donors and pharmaceutical companies ensure affordable and equitable access.
Incoming International AIDS Society (IAS) President Professor Kenneth Ngure of Kenya said scientific discoveries change lives only when they are translated into policies, financing and health services that reach the people who need them most.
Outlining his vision for the IAS, Ngure pledged to champion science, equity and the next generation of researchers while working to ensure that innovation benefits all countries, not just the wealthiest.
Despite the optimism surrounding these advances, concerns over funding dominated discussions throughout the conference.
Researchers, UN agencies and civil society organizations warned that the global HIV response is facing one of its most challenging financial periods in decades following significant cuts to international assistance, particularly from the United States.
Community organizations in several countries have already begun scaling back HIV prevention, testing and outreach services, raising fears that hard-won gains could be reversed.
New estimates presented during the conference showed that around 1.2 million people acquired HIV and 570,000 died from AIDS-related illnesses worldwide in 2025.
Experts warned those figures could rise if investment continues to decline.
The conference also highlighted how quickly HIV epidemics can expand when prevention programs weaken, citing Fiji as a stark example.
Researchers described Fiji as one of the world's fastest-growing HIV outbreaks, with new diagnoses rising sharply over the past five years, driven largely by injecting drug use. They urged the expansion of harm reduction measures, including needle and syringe programs, opioid substitution therapy and community-led interventions.
Throughout the week, speakers stressed that biomedical innovation alone will not end AIDS.
Success, they said, will also depend on protecting human rights, reducing stigma, strengthening community-led organizations and ensuring that key populations remain at the center of the response.
The discussions also carried important lessons for Bangladesh. Although the country remains a low-prevalence setting, much of its HIV prevention program—particularly services for people who inject drugs and other key populations—continues to rely on international donor support.
Experts said declining external financing makes greater domestic investment increasingly important to sustain prevention efforts and protect past achievements.
The conference also underscored the need for stronger collaboration between scientists, governments and communities, arguing that scientific breakthroughs have little value if they remain confined to laboratories instead of reaching the people who need them.
As the conference concluded, the International AIDS Society entered a new chapter with Kenneth Ngure assuming its presidency.
Ngure said the next phase of the global HIV response must focus not only on generating scientific evidence but also on translating discoveries into policies that improve lives through equitable access, stronger partnerships and investment in young researchers.
Delegates also looked ahead to the IAS Conference on HIV Science (IAS 2027), scheduled to be held in Geneva, Switzerland, from July 12 to 15, 2027, where scientists and policymakers will assess whether the commitments made in Rio have translated into tangible progress.

item.title: No respite for Dhaka consumers as food prices soar
item.description:
As households struggle to cope with rising living costs, there is little sign of relief in Dhaka's kitchen markets, where the prices of rice, vegetables, fish, eggs and poultry continue to edge higher.
After visiting several kitchen markets across Dhaka on Saturday, it was found that, except for a few varieties, almost all vegetables were selling for around Tk100 per kg, while green chilli prices had soared to Tk400 per kg.
Rice prices have also resumed their upward trend, with polao rice registering the sharpest increase. Traders said its price has jumped by Tk50–60 per kg within just a few days, adding to the burden on consumers already coping with a gas supply crisis.
According to traders, persistent rainfall and flooding in several parts of the country have submerged vegetable and chilli fields, disrupted supplies and increased transportation costs. The seasonal decline in supply during the monsoon has also contributed to higher prices of most essential commodities.
Fish prices have risen by Tk20–30 per kg over the past week. Pangas is now selling at Tk250 per kg, telapia at Tk280, rui at Tk300–450, pabda at Tk350–400, shrimp at Tk800–1,400, tengra at Tk700, indigenous koi at Tk700–800 and shoal at Tk700 per kg. Prices of bhetki, mrigel, baim, shing and poa fish have also increased.
Hilsa is being sold at Tk1,600–3,200 per kg, depending on its size and quality, while prices of sea fish have also climbed beyond the reach of many middle- and low-income consumers.
Anwar Hossain, a fish vendor at Dhupkhola Kitchen Market, said adverse weather has kept many fishing trawlers from going to sea, while supplies from different parts of the country have declined.
"Wholesale prices have increased due to lower supply, and that has inevitably pushed up retail prices," he said.
Consumers say persistently high food prices are forcing them to rethink their spending, with fish and meat becoming increasingly unaffordable.
"My children wanted to eat fish, but I was shocked by the prices at the market," said shopper Jony Sheikh. "I somehow managed to buy one fish for them. If prices keep rising, we'll have to cut back on fish and meat."
Green chilli prices have surged to Tk400 per kg across Dhaka's kitchen markets, up by around Tk100 from a week ago. Retailers are charging Tk40 for 100 grams and Tk100 for 250 grams.
Locally produced onions have also become costlier, rising by Tk15–20 per kg over the past one-and-a-half to two weeks. Depending on quality, they are now selling for Tk55–65 per kg.
Vegetable prices remain high, with long brinjal selling for Tk120–150 per kg, round brinjal Tk180, white brinjal Tk140, bitter gourd Tk120–140, yardlong beans Tk110–130, snake gourd Tk90–100 and taro corms Tk80–100 per kg. Only sponge gourd and pointed gourd offered some relief, with prices easing to Tk60–80 per kg. Rafique, a vegetable vendor, blamed the price hike on supply shortages caused by heavy rains and flooding.
"Supplies from different parts of the country have declined during the monsoon, while waterlogging has damaged chilli fields in major producing areas. Reduced supply has pushed up prices," he said.
Sridevi Biswas, a shopper at Ray Saheb Bazar, said she had planned to buy several vegetables but returned home with only one.
"I came to buy a few vegetables, but after seeing the prices I bought only one. If this trend continues, it will become even harder for middle-income families to manage their household expenses," she said. Egg prices have also moved up, with farm eggs now selling for Tk145–155 per dozen, compared with Tk135–140 a week ago.
Poultry prices also increased over the past day. Broiler chicken is now selling for Tk190–200 per kg, up from Tk180, while Sonali chicken has risen to Tk340–350 per kg from Tk330–340.
Robin Hasan, a university student living in a shared accommodation, said eggs and chicken had long been the most affordable protein options.
"Even those are becoming more expensive now. Managing within a limited budget is getting harder every day," he said.
While prices of coarse, medium-grade and Miniket rice have remained largely stable, polao rice has seen a sharp spike.
Coarse rice is selling for Tk58–65 per kg, medium-grade rice for Tk68–78, and Miniket and Nazirshail varieties for Tk80–95 per kg.
In contrast, polao rice, which sold for Tk120–140 per kg just a few days ago, is now priced at Tk180–200 per kg, marking an increase of Tk50–60 per kg.
Traders said the jump is the steepest increase in the rice market in recent weeks, adding to the financial strain on consumers already grappling with the rising cost of living.

item.title: NCP leader suspended over remarks about PM Tarique
item.description:
The National Citizen Party (NCP) has handed a fresh suspension to its central committee joint member secretary, Gazi Salahuddin Tanvir, days after he posted objectionable comments about Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on social media.
Tanvir was given a temporary suspension from his organizational post and served a show-cause notice on Friday night, hours after his controversial Facebook post drew widespread criticism.
He has been asked to submit a written defense, along with evidence and explanations, to the party's central disciplinary committee within two working days of receiving the notice, explaining why further organizational action should not be taken against him.
The post in question referenced attacks on and obstruction of NCP marches in three districts of Sylhet division, including Habiganj, in which Tanvir accused leaders of Chhatradal and Jubo Dal of involvement.
In the same post, he made the objectionable remarks about the prime minister. He deleted the post a few hours later amid backlash on Facebook, but screenshots of it continued to circulate on social media.
In a letter to Tanvir published on NCP's verified Facebook page Friday night, the party said a comment attributed to him was found to constitute "a serious organizational breach of discipline and damaging the party's image on social media."
The letter added that, given the gravity of the matter, he was being immediately relieved of his organizational responsibilities on the directives of NCP convener Nahid Islam and member secretary Akhter Hossen.
This marks the second time Tanvir has been suspended from the party. He was first removed in April 2025 following allegations that he interfered in deputy commissioner appointments after entering the secretariat in the aftermath of the July mass uprising and that he was involved in commission dealings related to textbook printing contracts with the National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB).
He remained outside the party for about a year before being reinstated on April 16 this year. His latest suspension comes roughly three and a half months after his return.
Shortly after the controversy broke, Tanvir posted on his own Facebook account expressing regret over his remarks.

item.title: Bangladesh's Sundarbans trail global tiger recovery
item.description:
The global wild tiger population is rebounding after decades of decline, driven by stronger conservation efforts and international cooperation. But conservationists say Bangladesh's Sundarbans, home to the country's only wild tiger population, faces unique ecological constraints that make rapid population growth far more difficult than in countries such as India and Nepal.
More than a century ago, an estimated 100,000 wild tigers roamed forests across Asia. By 2010, habitat destruction, poaching and the illegal wildlife trade had reduced that number to around 3,200, prompting the world's 13 tiger range countries to launch the ambitious TX2 initiative at the St. Petersburg Tiger Summit to double global tiger numbers.
According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), the Global Tiger Forum (GTF) and national wildlife authorities, the global wild tiger population has now recovered to an estimated 5,500–5,800 animals.
India remains the global leader in tiger conservation, hosting nearly three-quarters of the world's wild tigers. Its tiger population has risen from 1,411 in 2006 to more than 3,680, supported by protected reserves, connected wildlife corridors, intensive anti-poaching operations and sustained government investment.
Nepal has also emerged as one of the world's leading tiger conservation success stories. Its latest National Tiger Census, released on Global Tiger Day, recorded 429 wild tigers—up from 121 in 2009—following years of habitat restoration, scientific monitoring and community-based conservation across the Terai Arc Landscape.
Bangladesh's only wild tiger population survives in the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest shared with India.
Government camera-trap surveys have shown the country's tiger population increasing from 106 in 2015 to 114 in 2018 and an estimated 125 in 2024.
While the upward trend reflects progress in conservation efforts, experts caution against directly comparing Bangladesh's numbers with those of India or Nepal.
Dr Md Anwarul Islam, a wildlife conservationist and former professor of Zoology at the University of Dhaka, said the increase is encouraging but limited by the ecological characteristics of the Sundarbans.
"Our tiger population has increased from 106 in 2015 to 125 in 2024. This is undoubtedly positive, but the increase is modest compared with India, Nepal or Bhutan," he told Dhaka Tribune .
"The Sundarbans is a unique mangrove ecosystem. Unlike large inland forests, its ecological carrying capacity does not allow rapid expansion of tiger populations."
Unlike inland forests with abundant prey and expansive habitats, the Sundarbans can support only a limited number of tigers because of its mangrove ecosystem, experts say.
Islam said several human-induced pressures continue to weaken the forest's ecological balance.
"Illegal hunting of spotted deer, poisoning rivers and canals to catch fish, unsustainable extraction of forest resources and various human disturbances are reducing prey availability and affecting the habitat. Under these conditions, tiger reproduction cannot increase significantly."
He added that neighboring countries benefit from larger and better-connected forest landscapes that naturally support higher tiger populations.
"India, Nepal and Bhutan have larger landscapes and more favorable ecological conditions for tiger conservation. Those environmental advantages play a critical role in supporting larger tiger populations."
Islam said climate change poses an additional long-term threat to tiger conservation in the Sundarbans.
He noted that comparisons with India's overall tiger population can be misleading because the adjoining Indian Sundarbans have experienced similar ecological constraints.
"Many people compare Bangladesh's tiger population with India's national figures. However, if we specifically look at the Indian Sundarbans adjoining Bangladesh, tiger numbers have not increased dramatically there either."
"The two parts of the Sundarbans share similar challenges, including climate change, salinity intrusion, changing prey dynamics and other ecological pressures."
Scientists warn that rising sea levels, stronger cyclones, coastal erosion and increasing salinity are expected to reshape the Sundarbans ecosystem over the coming decades, making long-term tiger conservation increasingly challenging.
While India and Nepal have recorded significant gains, other tiger range countries present a mixed picture.
Russia has increased its Amur tiger population from around 40–50 animals in the 1940s to about 750 today. Bhutan's tiger population has grown from 103 in 2015 to more than 131, while Indonesia's Sumatra supports around 600 Sumatran tigers. Thailand is estimated to have between 180 and 220 wild tigers.
Elsewhere, however, tiger numbers continue to decline. Malaysia's population has fallen from nearly 3,000 several decades ago to fewer than 150 today. Myanmar is estimated to have only 20–30 wild tigers, while Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam have effectively lost their breeding tiger populations.
Conservationists say protecting tigers is about far more than increasing population numbers. As an apex predator, the tiger serves as an indicator of forest health, and safeguarding its habitat also protects biodiversity, freshwater resources and the livelihoods of millions of people who depend on forests.
For Bangladesh, experts say the long-term future of the Royal Bengal Tiger will depend not only on maintaining anti-poaching efforts but also on restoring prey populations, reducing human pressure, strengthening climate resilience and preserving the ecological integrity of the Sundarbans.
"The tiger is an umbrella species," Islam said. "If we can protect the tiger, we protect the entire Sundarbans ecosystem. The future of the tiger is inseparable from the future of the forest itself."

item.title: PM seeks stronger public-private partnership to boost economy
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday expressed optimism that Bangladesh's economy could undergo a positive transformation within the next 4-5 years if the government and the private sector work together to address existing challenges.
Speaking at an interactive session with private sector entrepreneurs, the prime minister said: "There are problems in some areas, but if we work together, we can overcome them."
The nearly 4-hour meeting began around 10am at the Prime Minister's Office in Tejgaon. It was organized by the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA), according to Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu.
According to Shiplu, the discussions focused on business expansion, attracting greater foreign investment and creating a more conducive environment for industrialization.

item.title: Four killed in pickup-truck collision in Bogra
item.description:
Four people, including a pickup van driver, were killed in a head-on collision between a pickup van and a goods-laden truck in Bogra's Kahaloo upazila on Saturday morning.
The accident occurred in the Kazipara Boubazar area of Birkedar union along the Bogra–Naogaon highway.
The deceased were identified as Toriqul Islam Riyad, 23, son of Ferdous Islam of Pachashi village in Gouripur upazila; pickup driver Nasir Uddin, 24, son of the late Amin Khan of the same village; Lutfor Rahman, 50, son of Toyeb Ali of Raghabpur in Mymensingh Sadar; and Shubha Debnath, 23, son of Chittaranjan Debnath of the same area.
According to family members, the three fish traders had travelled from Mymensingh to Adamdighi in Bogra with a consignment of fish fry for sale. After selling the fish, they were returning home when the accident occurred.
Police said the crash occurred around 10:00 am when the pickup van attempted to overtake a bus and collided head-on with a Naogaon-bound truck coming from the opposite direction, killing the driver and three fish traders on the spot.
The accident briefly disrupted traffic on the Bogra–Naogaon highway. Fire Service and Civil Defence personnel, assisted by police, recovered the bodies and removed the wrecked vehicles, allowing traffic to resume.
Sub-Inspector Brojer Mahato of Kahaloo Police Station said the victims included three fish traders and the pickup driver. The pickup van and the truck have been seized, while the truck driver and his assistant fled the scene.
"The victims' families in Mymensingh have been informed. The bodies will be handed over to their relatives upon arrival," he said.
Officer-in-Charge (OC) Shafiqul Islam said a case has been filed under the Road Transport Act, and efforts are underway to arrest the absconding truck driver.

item.title: Dengue cases rise by 371 in 24 hours
item.description:
Health authorities on Saturday reported 371 new dengue cases across Bangladesh in the 24 hours preceding Saturday morning, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
According to a DGHS statement, 91 patients were admitted to hospitals in Chittagong division, 69 in Barisal division, 57 in Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC), 46 in Dhaka division, 34 in Khulna division, 32 in Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC), 23 in Mymensingh division, 17 in Rajshahi division, and 2 in Sylhet division.
With the latest figures, the country has recorded 15,681 dengue cases and 54 deaths so far this year.
Last year, dengue claimed 413 lives and infected 102,861 people across the country.
In 2024, dengue caused 575 deaths and infected 101,214 people.

item.title: 14,384 primary teachers to join from October
item.description:
The Ministry of Primary and Mass Education has said the joining process for 14,384 recommended assistant teachers for government primary schools will begin within October, ending months of uncertainty over their appointments.
The announcement came after an emergency virtual meeting on teacher recruitment held at the ministry on Saturday, according to a message issued by the ministry the same day.
Primary and Mass Education Secretary Shakhawat Hossain said the government is prioritizing the joining of the 14,384 recommended assistant teachers for primary schools, adding that the process had been delayed due to investigation and procedural complexities.
"The joining process will begin by the upcoming October 30," he said.
More than 175 days have passed since the publication of the final results, yet the 14,384 selected candidates are yet to receive their appointment letters. The candidates had earlier demanded that the joining notification be issued by July 29.
With that deadline passing without any notification, the job aspirants had announced a fresh round of continuous sit-in demonstrations at Shahbagh from Sunday.

item.title: Bangladesh drawn with Sri Lanka, Bhutan in SAFF Championship
item.description:
Hosts Bangladesh have been drawn in Group A alongside Sri Lanka and Bhutan for the 2026 SAFF Championship, with Nepal set to join the group if FIFA lifts its suspension before the tournament.
The draw for the 15th edition of South Asia's premier international football tournament was held in Thimphu, Bhutan, on Saturday.
As hosts, Bangladesh were placed in Group A, while regional powerhouse and defending champions India were seeded separately in Group B as the highest-ranked South Asian nation, ensuring the two sides cannot meet before the knockout stage.
Bangladesh's group currently features Sri Lanka and Bhutan, but SAFF confirmed Nepal will be included if FIFA lifts the suspension on the All Nepal Football Association by September 1. If the ban remains in place, the tournament will proceed with six teams.
Group B comprises defending champions India, the Maldives and Pakistan.
The championship will be staged in Dhaka from November 4 to 17, marking Bangladesh's first time hosting the tournament since 2018. The top two teams from each group will advance to the semi-finals, scheduled for November 14, with the final set for November 17.
Bangladesh will look to end a 23-year wait for their second SAFF title, having lifted the trophy only once in 2003. The hosts are expected to field a strengthened squad featuring expatriate footballers such as Hamza Choudhury and Shamit Shome as they bid to capitalise on home advantage.
The tournament, originally scheduled for 2025, was postponed by a year before SAFF confirmed Bangladesh as the host nation earlier this year.

Celebrated mountaineer Nirmal Purja die in avalanche in Pakistan
item.description:
NEPAL-PAKISTAN/CLIMBERS

Celebrated Nepali climber Nirmal Purja, who set a record for the fastest ascent of the world''s 14 highest mountains, died in an avalanche during an expedition in Pakistan, his company said on Saturday.

“Today it is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ''Nimsdai'' Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak,” his expedition organising company Elite Exped said in an Instagram post.

“We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive,” it added, without giving details.

Purja, 43, and nine others had been missing since Thursday after being struck by an avalanche on the 8,051-metre (26,414-foot) Broad Peak, the world's 12th-highest mountain, a technically difficult climb in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan region.

Officials said the bodies of Purja and other climbers were located in a difficult site and had yet to be retrieved.

Purja, who served in the British military with the Gurkhas and later in special forces, completed the record-breaking feat in six months in 2019. He became widely known internationally after the Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible," was released two years later.

The 10 mountaineers were caught in an avalanche around midday on Thursday. Six of the 10 were Nepalis and the others were from ⁠Pakistan, Oman, the US and China.

Search crews recovered three bodies on Friday.

Chhang Dawa Sherpa, a board director of Seven Summit Treks which had three Sherpa guides among the dead ⁠climbers, said the remaining bodies were "spotted and identified" with the help of drone footage and were yet to be retrieved.

"They are in a difficult spot and have not been retrieved yet," Chhang told Reuters.

He said that unlike Nepal, Pakistan does not have the practice of long-line rescue by helicopters on the mountains.

"We have to take into account the safety of those who go and retrieve the bodies."

Sajid Hussain, deputy director of the tourism department of Gilgit-Baltistan region of Pakistan, said the rescue operation was still ongoing.

"Rescue teams have successfully identified the location of the victims; however, they have not yet been able to recover and bring them down safely," he told Reuters.

"Although the location has been confirmed, the recovery mission has not yet been successful."

Hussain said this is an "extremely challenging" mountain recovery operation that requires rescuers to climb to the site.

While drone surveillance and aerial reconnaissance have helped identify the exact location, reaching the victims and safely recovering them remains a highly difficult task, he said.

In 2019, Purja climbed Annapurna, the 10th-highest mountain in the world. He then began taking on other 8,000-metre peaks. Of the world's 14 highest mountains, eight are in ⁠Nepal, five in Pakistan and one in the Tibet region of China.

Climbing experts say barely more than three dozen mountaineers have climbed all 14 peaks to date. Broad Peak is considered one of Pakistan''s most challenging climbs.

item.title: Dhaka at 416: Bigger city, deeper crises
item.description:
As Dhaka steps into its 416th year, the city faces a sobering reality: decades of rapid, largely unplanned urbanization have left Bangladesh's capital increasingly congested, polluted and environmentally fragile, with experts warning that its future livability is at growing risk unless long-delayed reforms are implemented.
Once celebrated as a city of rivers, canals and open spaces, Dhaka is now struggling with disappearing waterways, shrinking green cover, hazardous air pollution, chronic traffic congestion and overstretched infrastructure -- problems urban planners say have accumulated over decades of weak planning and poor enforcement.
The anniversary coincides with the week-long "Hridoye Dhaka" festival, organized by Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) from August 1 to 7, featuring cultural performances, heritage walks and exhibitions celebrating the city's history.
But urban planners argue the milestone should serve not only as a celebration of Dhaka's past, but also as a reminder of the urgent challenges threatening its future.
Historically, Mughal Subahdar Islam Khan declared Dhaka the provincial capital of Bengal in 1610, while the establishment of the Dhaka Municipality on August 1, 1864 laid the foundation for modern urban governance.
Perhaps the clearest sign of the city's declining livability is the rapid disappearance of green spaces.
A study published in the Elsevier journal Environmental Challenges found that Dhaka lost 56% of its green cover between 1989 and 2020, around 7,146 hectares, while healthy vegetation declined from 17% of the city's area to just 2%.
Urban planners attribute the decline to unplanned development, weak enforcement and inadequate protection of public open spaces.
Akhtar Mahmud, adviser to the Bangladesh Institute of Planners (BIP), said repeated public protests and court interventions had failed to stop the destruction of parks and playgrounds.
"The continued loss of urban green spaces reflects a failure of governance despite years of public resistance and court interventions to protect places such as Suhrawardy Udyan, Dhanmondi Math, Tetultala, Balur Math and Anwara Park," he said.
The city's natural drainage system has also steadily disappeared.
Although official records list between 46 and 50 canals, studies by the Institute of Water Modelling (IWM) and the Joint Canal Recovery Taskforce suggest that only 26 to 38 remain functional or capable of restoration.
Many have been encroached upon, filled up or reduced to narrow drains.
Urban planners say this loss is one of the main reasons Dhaka now suffers severe waterlogging after even moderate rainfall.
Former Bangladesh Institute of Planners president Adil Mohammad Khan said restoring canals would require political commitment and decisive legal action against encroachers.
"If authorities take legal action against canal encroachers, it will send a strong message," he said, adding that no restoration initiative would succeed without recovering the city's waterways.
Experts note that healthy cities should retain roughly 15% of their land as wetlands or water bodies, while Dhaka's Flood Action Plan recommends at least 12%. The capital now falls well below those thresholds.
Environmental degradation is also exacting a growing public health and economic cost.
Research led by Jahangirnagar University scientist Dr Md Sakhaoat Hossain, published in Population and Environment , estimates that fine particulate pollution (PM2.5) contributes to around 88,240 premature deaths annually across Bangladesh.
The study estimates the economic losses associated with air pollution at nearly $23 billion each year, equivalent to roughly 5% of the country's GDP.
Traffic congestion has become another defining feature of life in the capital.
According to the World Bank's 2025 project appraisal document, traffic congestion costs Dhaka approximately 3.2 million working hours every day, reducing productivity, increasing fuel consumption and worsening the quality of urban life.
Urban planners say that without expanding reliable public transport, protecting remaining open spaces, restoring canals and enforcing long-term urban planning, Dhaka's environmental and infrastructure crises will continue to deepen.
As the city marks another year of its long history, they argue that the greatest challenge is no longer preserving its heritage, but ensuring that future generations inherit a capital that remains livable.

item.title: CTTC rules out link between Motijheel explosive, Mirpur-Farmgate incidents
item.description:
The Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) unit of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) on Saturday said the explosive recovered beneath Motijheel Metro Rail Station last week was not linked to the bomb-like objects reported at the Mirpur-10 and Farmgate metro stations earlier in the day.
At a press briefing on Saturday, CTTC Chief and DMP Additional Police Commissioner Mohammad Shamsul Haque said the investigation had found no link between the Motijheel explosive recovery and the two incidents.
"So far, we have found no link between the explosive recovered at Motijheel and the bomb-like objects found at Mirpur-10 and Farmgate. The investigation is ongoing, and all necessary measures are being taken," he said.
Responding to a question, Shamsul Haque said the bag recovered at Mirpur-10 Metro Rail Station contained betel leaves, areca nuts, zarda and other everyday items, while the sack found at Farmgate contained discarded waste.
"No explosives were found at either location. As such, the two incidents are being treated as isolated cases," he said.
Asked whether any criminal group was behind the incidents, he said it would not be appropriate to comment before the investigation is completed.
Replying to another question on whether there was any militant involvement, he said no comments could be made until the investigation is over.
On the progress of the Motijheel explosive recovery case, the CTTC chief said police, CTTC and the Detective Branch (DB) are jointly investigating the incident and any new findings will be shared with the media.
Regarding the unavailability of CCTV footage or cameras being out of service at different locations, he said all related issues, including CCTV footage, are under investigation and the matter would become clearer after the inquiry is completed.
Referring to reports of bomb scares across the capital, Shamsul Haque urged people not to panic, saying police take precautionary measures whenever any suspicious object is reported.
He also called on people to refrain from spreading rumours or unnecessary panic.
Earlier, in his written statement, Shamsul Haque said the CTTC Bomb Disposal Unit responded immediately after receiving reports of bomb-like objects at Mirpur-10 Metro Rail Station and Farmgate on Saturday.
After conducting examinations using modern equipment, the unit confirmed that neither of the recovered objects contained explosives.
He said the bag recovered at Mirpur-10 contained betel leaf, areca nut, zarda and other ordinary items, while the sack found at Farmgate contained discarded waste, posing no threat to public safety.
Shamsul Haque also noted that the CTTC Bomb Disposal Unit had earlier professionally handled the recovery of an explosive-like object beneath Motijheel Metro Rail Station, ensuring public safety.
Urging people not to be misled by rumours or misinformation, he requested the public not to touch any suspicious object. Instead, they should maintain a safe distance and immediately inform the nearest police station, the national emergency service 999, or law enforcement agencies.
He also sought public cooperation by sharing necessary information to help ensure public safety.

item.title: No respite for Dhaka consumers as food prices soar
item.description:
As households struggle to cope with rising living costs, there is little sign of relief in Dhaka's kitchen markets, where the prices of rice, vegetables, fish, eggs and poultry continue to edge higher.
After visiting several kitchen markets across Dhaka on Saturday, it was found that, except for a few varieties, almost all vegetables were selling for around Tk100 per kg, while green chilli prices had soared to Tk400 per kg.
Rice prices have also resumed their upward trend, with polao rice registering the sharpest increase. Traders said its price has jumped by Tk50–60 per kg within just a few days, adding to the burden on consumers already coping with a gas supply crisis.
According to traders, persistent rainfall and flooding in several parts of the country have submerged vegetable and chilli fields, disrupted supplies and increased transportation costs. The seasonal decline in supply during the monsoon has also contributed to higher prices of most essential commodities.
Fish prices have risen by Tk20–30 per kg over the past week. Pangas is now selling at Tk250 per kg, telapia at Tk280, rui at Tk300–450, pabda at Tk350–400, shrimp at Tk800–1,400, tengra at Tk700, indigenous koi at Tk700–800 and shoal at Tk700 per kg. Prices of bhetki, mrigel, baim, shing and poa fish have also increased.
Hilsa is being sold at Tk1,600–3,200 per kg, depending on its size and quality, while prices of sea fish have also climbed beyond the reach of many middle- and low-income consumers.
Anwar Hossain, a fish vendor at Dhupkhola Kitchen Market, said adverse weather has kept many fishing trawlers from going to sea, while supplies from different parts of the country have declined.
"Wholesale prices have increased due to lower supply, and that has inevitably pushed up retail prices," he said.
Consumers say persistently high food prices are forcing them to rethink their spending, with fish and meat becoming increasingly unaffordable.
"My children wanted to eat fish, but I was shocked by the prices at the market," said shopper Jony Sheikh. "I somehow managed to buy one fish for them. If prices keep rising, we'll have to cut back on fish and meat."
Green chilli prices have surged to Tk400 per kg across Dhaka's kitchen markets, up by around Tk100 from a week ago. Retailers are charging Tk40 for 100 grams and Tk100 for 250 grams.
Locally produced onions have also become costlier, rising by Tk15–20 per kg over the past one-and-a-half to two weeks. Depending on quality, they are now selling for Tk55–65 per kg.
Vegetable prices remain high, with long brinjal selling for Tk120–150 per kg, round brinjal Tk180, white brinjal Tk140, bitter gourd Tk120–140, yardlong beans Tk110–130, snake gourd Tk90–100 and taro corms Tk80–100 per kg. Only sponge gourd and pointed gourd offered some relief, with prices easing to Tk60–80 per kg. Rafique, a vegetable vendor, blamed the price hike on supply shortages caused by heavy rains and flooding.
"Supplies from different parts of the country have declined during the monsoon, while waterlogging has damaged chilli fields in major producing areas. Reduced supply has pushed up prices," he said.
Sridevi Biswas, a shopper at Ray Saheb Bazar, said she had planned to buy several vegetables but returned home with only one.
"I came to buy a few vegetables, but after seeing the prices I bought only one. If this trend continues, it will become even harder for middle-income families to manage their household expenses," she said. Egg prices have also moved up, with farm eggs now selling for Tk145–155 per dozen, compared with Tk135–140 a week ago.
Poultry prices also increased over the past day. Broiler chicken is now selling for Tk190–200 per kg, up from Tk180, while Sonali chicken has risen to Tk340–350 per kg from Tk330–340.
Robin Hasan, a university student living in a shared accommodation, said eggs and chicken had long been the most affordable protein options.
"Even those are becoming more expensive now. Managing within a limited budget is getting harder every day," he said.
While prices of coarse, medium-grade and Miniket rice have remained largely stable, polao rice has seen a sharp spike.
Coarse rice is selling for Tk58–65 per kg, medium-grade rice for Tk68–78, and Miniket and Nazirshail varieties for Tk80–95 per kg.
In contrast, polao rice, which sold for Tk120–140 per kg just a few days ago, is now priced at Tk180–200 per kg, marking an increase of Tk50–60 per kg.
Traders said the jump is the steepest increase in the rice market in recent weeks, adding to the financial strain on consumers already grappling with the rising cost of living.

item.title: Police HQ issues nationwide highest alert over threat to police vehicles
item.description:
Police Headquarters on Saturday placed all police units across the country on the highest level of alert following intelligence reports of possible sabotage targeting police vehicles.
In a directive issued to field-level units, Police Headquarters said intelligence indicated that members of extremist groups or other miscreants could target police jeeps, pickup vans, buses and other official vehicles.
The directive stressed that there must be no complacency or negligence in ensuring the security of police vehicles and instructed officers to maintain maximum vigilance both during operations and after vehicles are parked.
It said any police vehicle making a temporary stop while on duty must be parked only in a secure location and remain under constant supervision. Vehicles must not be left unattended unless the driver or the designated responsible officer is present.
The directive also ordered enhanced security for government vehicles kept at police stations, police lines, office compounds and other designated locations after duty hours.
It further instructed all units to conduct regular patrols, strengthen surveillance and remain alert to any suspicious persons or objects around parked vehicles.
Describing the matter as "highly important," Police Headquarters directed all metropolitan, range, district and other field-level police units to strictly implement the security measures.

item.title: Industry-academia partnership discussed at HR Summit 2026
item.description:
Leading human resource professionals, corporate executives, and academics on Saturday emphasized strengthening long-term partnerships between industry and higher education institutions to address the challenges posed by the Fourth Industrial Revolution, artificial intelligence (AI), and the evolving global labor market.
The speakers made the remarks at HR Summit 2026: "Empowering Today's Talent to Lead Tomorrow," organized by the Center for Career Development (CCD) of Green University of Bangladesh at the university campus.
They said Bangladesh's young population must be equipped with future-ready skills, effective leadership, and employment-oriented competencies to remain globally competitive.
The day-long summit brought together more than 30 human resource (HR) professionals, corporate executives, academics, administrative officials, students, and young professionals. It featured 3 panel discussions and 2 roundtable sessions on the future workforce, leadership development, employability skills, talent management, technology-driven HR management, workplace transformation in the age of AI, and industry-academia collaboration.
Speakers throughout the event said closer collaboration between universities and industry is essential to bridge the gap between academic learning and workplace requirements.
Delivering the keynote address, Vice Chancellor of Green University of Bangladesh Professor Dr Mohammad Shorif Uddin said: "The HR Summit is not merely an event; it is an effective platform for building long-term partnerships between the university and the corporate sector. Our goal is not only to award degrees but also to develop our students into successful professionals and future leaders."
Pro Vice Chancellor of Green University of Bangladesh Professor Dr Khawza Iftekhar Uddin Ahmed, the special guest, said: "Alongside technical knowledge, effective communication skills, creativity, and leadership are the fundamental pillars of a student's career development. This summit will provide valuable new directions for our students."
HR experts at the summit said lifelong learning and continuous skill development have become increasingly important as technology advances. They added that strengthening the professional skills, career readiness, and leadership capabilities of Bangladesh's youth would support sustainable economic growth and improve the country's global competitiveness.
The panel discussions and roundtable sessions included senior executives, HR leaders, and industry experts from various organizations, including ABM Yusuf Ali Khan of Aman Group, Sheikh Aminur Rahman of Prime Bank FinTech Limited, Ashfaqur Rahman of Kazi & Kazi Tea Estate Ltd, and Zia Uddin Mahmud of Creative Business Group.
Participants also took part in interactive discussions and question-and-answer sessions on contemporary HR challenges, future opportunities, and workplace innovation.
The summit concluded with the presentation of commemorative awards to the speakers and panelists.

item.title: Does coffee really raise blood pressure?
item.description:
For millions of people, the day doesn't truly begin until that first sip of coffee. Whether it's a steaming mug at sunrise or an afternoon latte to beat the slump, coffee is woven into daily routines around the world. Yet for people living with high blood pressure, every cup can come with a lingering question: Is coffee helping—or harming—the heart?
The answer is more nuanced than a simple yes or no.
While caffeine can cause a temporary rise in blood pressure, research suggests that moderate coffee consumption is unlikely to pose a significant risk for most healthy adults. The key lies in understanding how caffeine affects the body, how much you drink, and whether you already have underlying health conditions.
Why blood pressure rises after coffee
Coffee's stimulating effect comes from caffeine, which activates the nervous system and triggers the release of adrenaline. This hormone causes the heart to beat faster and blood vessels to constrict temporarily, leading to a short-term increase in blood pressure.
The effect tends to be more noticeable in people who rarely consume caffeine or those with existing hypertension. For regular coffee drinkers, however, the body often develops a degree of tolerance, making the blood pressure response less pronounced over time.
Understanding blood pressure
Blood pressure measures the force of blood pushing against the walls of the arteries as the heart pumps. A reading of around 120/80 mmHg is generally considered normal, while consistently elevated readings may indicate hypertension.
Often called the "silent killer," high blood pressure frequently develops without obvious symptoms. If left untreated, it can increase the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, and other cardiovascular complications.
How long does caffeine's effect last?
The rise in blood pressure usually begins within 30 minutes of consuming coffee, peaks within one to two hours, and may last for several hours. Exactly how long the effects persist depends on factors such as age, genetics, medications, metabolism, and how frequently a person consumes caffeine.
Because individuals process caffeine differently, the same cup of coffee may have little effect on one person while causing a noticeable spike in another.
What the research says
Studies have shown that caffeine-containing products—including coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks, and even chocolate—can temporarily increase blood pressure. In general, systolic blood pressure may rise by about 3 to 15 mmHg, while diastolic pressure may increase by roughly 4 to 13 mmHg shortly after caffeine consumption.
For most healthy adults, these changes are temporary and do not appear to translate into a substantially higher long-term risk of cardiovascular disease from moderate coffee consumption alone.
However, people with uncontrolled hypertension, heart disease, or certain other medical conditions should speak with their healthcare provider about how much caffeine is appropriate for them.
So, should you stop drinking coffee?
Not necessarily.
Most health experts agree that moderate coffee consumption can be part of a healthy lifestyle for many people, including those with well-controlled blood pressure. Rather than eliminating coffee altogether, it is more important to pay attention to how your body responds.
If you notice your blood pressure rises significantly after drinking coffee—or if your hypertension is difficult to control—your healthcare provider may recommend reducing your caffeine intake or avoiding it before blood pressure measurements.
The bottom line
Coffee can cause a temporary increase in blood pressure, especially in people who are sensitive to caffeine or who consume it only occasionally. But for most people, enjoying coffee in moderation is unlikely to have a major impact on long-term heart health.
If you have high blood pressure, monitor your readings regularly, maintain a heart-healthy lifestyle, and consult your healthcare provider if you're unsure how caffeine fits into your diet. For many people, the issue isn't whether to give up coffee—it's knowing how much is right for them.

item.title: Rainy season fruits that can help strengthen your immunity
item.description:
The arrival of the monsoon brings welcome relief from the summer heat, but it also creates ideal conditions for seasonal illnesses. High humidity, sudden temperature changes, and waterborne and airborne infections become more common during this time of year, making it important to pay extra attention to overall health.
While good hygiene, safe drinking water, and freshly prepared meals remain essential, your daily fruit bowl can also play a valuable role. Seasonal fruits are packed with vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, and fiber that help support the immune system and keep the body nourished. Here are five fruits worth adding to your diet this rainy season.
Jamun: A monsoon superfruit
Java plum, locally known as jamun , is one of the season's most distinctive fruits. Rich in vitamin C, iron, and anthocyanins—natural compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties— jamun helps support immune function while promoting gut health. Its unique sweet-tart flavor also makes it a refreshing seasonal treat.
Papaya: Gentle on the stomach, good for immunity
Papaya is widely available throughout the monsoon and offers far more than its naturally sweet taste. It is an excellent source of vitamins A and C and contains papain, a digestive enzyme that helps break down proteins and supports healthy digestion. Since a healthy gut plays an important role in immune function, papaya is a smart addition to a balanced diet.
Pear: Hydration with every bite
Often overlooked, pears are packed with water and dietary fiber, making them an excellent choice for staying hydrated and maintaining digestive health. They also provide vitamin C, adding another layer of nutritional support during the rainy season.
Pomegranate: Packed with protective nutrients
Known for its vibrant ruby-red seeds, pomegranate is rich in vitamin C and polyphenols—plant compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress. Regularly including pomegranate in your diet can help support normal immune function while adding a burst of flavor to salads, yogurt, or fresh fruit bowls.
Apple: A timeless healthy choice
Apples remain one of the easiest and most nutritious fruits to enjoy year-round, including during the monsoon. They contain quercetin, an antioxidant associated with immune health, along with dietary fiber that nourishes beneficial gut bacteria. Whether eaten on their own or added to breakfast, apples make a simple yet nutritious addition to everyday meals.
Eat smart this monsoon
No single fruit can prevent illness, but a diet rich in seasonal produce can help support your body's natural defenses. Pair these nutrient-rich fruits with proper hygiene, adequate hydration, sufficient sleep, regular physical activity, and freshly prepared meals to stay healthy throughout the rainy season.
This monsoon, embracing seasonal fruits isn't just about enjoying their fresh flavors—it's a simple, delicious way to nourish your body and build healthy habits that last well beyond the rains.

item.title: Cotton cultivation holds strong potential in Bangladesh; coordinated action, incentives needed
item.description:
Experts have called for coordinated action to expand cotton cultivation in Bangladesh, highlighting its potential as a climate-adaptive and economically viable crop.

They noted that although Bangladesh is the world's second-largest exporter of ready-made garments, around 97 per cent of the cotton used by the country's textile industry is imported, costing the country more than USD 3 billion annually.

These observations were made at the National Dialogue on Cotton: Its Future Opportunities as a Climate Adaptive Crop, organised by BRAC's Climate and Environmental Innovation Programme (CEIP) at the BRAC Centre in Mohakhali, Dhaka, 30 July 2026, said a press release.

The dialogue examined the structural barriers to expanding domestic cotton production and explored practical measures relating to policy, research, financing, agricultural extension services, market development, and post-harvest management.

Speaking at the event, Md Rezaul Amin, Executive Director (Routine Duties) of the Cotton Development Board, said that cotton is a beneficial crop from multiple perspectives. In addition to increasing farmers' incomes, cotton cultivation can contribute to climate change adaptation and generate employment opportunities across the value chain. He added that the government is providing incentives to encourage farmers to cultivate cotton.

Md Liakath Ali, Director of BRAC's Climate and Environmental Innovation Programme (CEIP) and Disaster Risk Management Programme (DRMP), said that cotton offers a promising alternative in areas where agricultural production has been affected by climate change.

He emphasised that expanding cotton cultivation across the country would require close collaboration among government agencies, the private sector, development organisations, and other stakeholders.

M Farid Uddin, Senior Agronomic Adviser/Consultant at CottonConnect South Asia Private Limited and former Executive Director of the Cotton Development Board, said that Bangladesh currently cultivates cotton on approximately 45,000 hectares of land, producing an estimated 200,000 bales annually (each bale weighing 220 kilograms), meeting only around 2 per cent of national demand.

He also noted that cotton is a carbon-positive crop and that the government officially declared cotton an agricultural commodity one year ago.

Among those attending the event was Mitali Chakma, a cotton farmer from Manikchhari in Rangamati. She said, "I received seeds and training from the Cotton Development Board. I have been cultivating cotton for the past three years. There is considerable interest in cotton cultivation among farmers. With the necessary support, cotton cultivation can expand significantly across the Chattogram Hill Tracts."

Participants observed that the challenges facing cotton production extend beyond cultivation itself. Cotton competes with rice, tobacco, and high-value winter vegetables for agricultural land.

Harvesting remains largely manual, while farmers continue to face constraints in accessing finance, agricultural inputs, extension services, storage facilities, ginning services, and reliable markets.

The discussion also highlighted the significant potential for cotton cultivation in climate-vulnerable regions, including the Barind Tract, coastal saline areas, riverine chars, and the Chattogram Hill Tracts.

As a heat- and drought-tolerant crop, cotton requires less water than rice, making it a suitable option for climate adaptation and livelihood diversification. Participants also noted that replacing tobacco cultivation with cotton in selected regions could provide farmers with a more sustainable alternative.

The dialogue opened with remarks by Abu Sadat Moniruzzaman Khan, Programme Head, Climate and Environmental Innovation Programme (CEIP), BRAC.

Other speakers included Abed Chaudhury, Independent Agro-specialist; Md Kutub Uddin, Deputy Director (HQ), Cotton Development Board; Md. Manirul Islam, Additional Director (Cash Crop), Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE); and Prof. Mohammad Kamrul Hasan, Professor (Department of Agroforestry), Bangladesh Agricultural University.

Representatives from Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council (BARC), Bangladesh Agricultural University (BAU), Bank Asia, Primark, WeGro, and other organisations also participated in the dialogue.

item.title: If it was a courtesy call, that's a different matter: Jamaat chief on Gor-Trivedi meeting
item.description:
US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia and US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor is on a three-day visit to Dhaka. During the visit, he met Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi at a hotel in the capital on Friday. Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Shafiqur Rahman, however, has reacted to the meeting.

Responding to a question from journalists, the Jamaat chief said: “They (Sergio Gor and Dinesh Trivedi) can talk in India. He (Sergio Gor) is the ambassador to India. If he came here and met the high commissioner (Dinesh Trivedi) as a courtesy call, then that is a different matter. But if the discussion involved any issue concerning the two countries, it should have been held with the (Bangladesh) government and with the opposition parties. It is not something we expect to take place with the diplomat of any particular country.”

He made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists after attending the anniversary programme of the Sylhet-based Daily Jalalabad on Saturday afternoon. Earlier, he addressed the newspaper's 34th anniversary event as the chief guest at a gathering of distinguished guests.

Referring to the government's recent appointment of Md Shamsul Alam, a retired official, as a deputy secretary at the Election Commission Secretariat, the Jamaat chief said: “The government has started certain processes that concern us. A party-affiliated person who retired five to seven years ago has been appointed to the Election Commission. He is a core party loyalist. Looking back at the previous election held on 12 February 2026, we are already worried. If such manoeuvres continue, the entire nation will question the government's sincerity regarding the election. If there is any attempt to stage such an election again, neither the people nor we will accept it.”

Shafiqur Rahman also urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to take responsibility for curbing corruption. According to him, Tarique Rahman is both the head of the government and the head of the BNP, and therefore must also take responsibility for controlling his party.

He said, “The prime minister belongs to the whole country. He must take responsibility, stop corruption and end extortion. Even the Speaker has said that unless extortion is stopped, the nation faces the risk of serious consequences in the near future.

“We do not want our country to sink once again into quicksand and dark alleys.”

The Jamaat chief also alleged that the BNP changed its position on holding a referendum after securing an overwhelming majority in parliament. He said: “Everyone had supported a referendum. Why did they suddenly change their position? After securing a two-thirds majority, they thought they could do whatever they wanted. They then decided that accepting a referendum would create problems for them, so there was no need for it. History in this country, and across the world, shows what happens when the people's verdict is not respected. The consequences are extremely grave.”

Earlier, speaking as the chief guest at a gathering marking the anniversary of Jalalabad at Kudrat Ullah Mosque Market in Bandar Bazar, Sylhet, he said: “The country's biggest crisis today is the crisis of trust. Unless we restore that trust, we will not be able to stand tall as a nation. The countries with the strongest passports are the ones that command the greatest respect. Citizens of those countries can travel to the largest number of destinations without a visa. In that regard, our position is extremely weak.”

The gathering was chaired by Jalalabad editor and Sylhet Press Club president Muktabis Un Noor. Among the special guests were Rajesh Bhatia, second secretary at the Assistant High Commission of India in Sylhet; Abdur Rob, vice-chancellor of Manarat International University; Imdad Hossain Chowdhury, general secretary of Sylhet Metropolitan BNP; Muhammad Fakhrul Islam, ameer of Sylhet Metropolitan Jamaat; Habibur Rahman, ameer of Sylhet district Jamaat; Abdul Hannan, vice-chairman of Jalalabad Syndicate Private Limited; and Mohammad Sirajul Islam, secretary of the Sylhet Press Club.

item.description:
The BNP on Saturday entrusted party Chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman with the authority to finalize the party's candidate for the upcoming presidential election.
The decision was taken at a meeting of the party's National Standing Committee held at the BNP chairman's Gulshan office in the evening.
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, BNP Secretary General Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir said the Standing Committee authorized Tarique Rahman to make all decisions regarding the party's presidential nominee and the election process.
"On behalf of the party, we have entrusted all responsibilities relating to the selection of the presidential candidate and the election to our Chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman," Fakhrul said.
He said the Standing Committee also discussed the government's development activities, the upcoming local government elections, and organizational matters.
The meeting, which began at 8pm, was chaired by Tarique Rahman.
Fakhrul and BNP Standing Committee members Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain, Gayeshwar Chandra Roy, Nazrul Islam Khan, Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Salahuddin Ahmed, Selima Rahman, Iqbal Hassan Mahmood Tuku, and Prof Dr AZM Zahid Hossain were present at the meeting.
Speaking after the meeting, Salahuddin said the Election Commission is legally required to hold the presidential election within 90 days and has already indicated its readiness to conduct the polls.
"Once the Election Commission announces the election schedule, our party chairman will finalize the candidate. The Standing Committee has entrusted him with that responsibility," he said.
Asked whether the party discussed any specific names for the presidency, Salahuddin replied, "No, no names were discussed."
On July 24 last, Mohammed Shahabuddin resigned as president, and Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad took charge as the acting president.
According to Article 123(2) of the Constitution, an election to fill the vacant office of the president must be held within 90 days of the post becoming vacant due to resignation.
The president shall be elected by members of Parliament for a five-year term. item.title: Chinese Economic Zone in Chattogram: USD 1.3b investment, over 100,000 jobs expected
item.description:
A Chinese Economic and Industrial Zone is set to be developed on 783 acres of land in Anwara, Chattogram, strategically located between Chittagong Port to the north, the Karnaphuli Tunnel and Shah Amanat International Airport nearby, and the under-construction Matarbari Deep-Sea Port to the south.

According to the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA), the zone is expected to attract USD 1.3 billion in investment—equivalent to about Tk 160 billion—and create more than 100,000 direct and indirect jobs.

The zone's greatest advantage is its location. Anwara is directly connected to Chittagong Port through the Karnaphuli Tunnel. Meanwhile, a new road linking Anwara to Matarbari via Banshkhali and Pekua has been planned. Once completed, it will integrate the industrial zone with both Chittagong Port and the future Matarbari Deep-Sea Port, creating an efficient industrial and freight transport network.

Business leaders, however, caution that geographical proximity alone will not ensure industrialisation. They stress that road connectivity, gas, electricity, water, waste management and fast investment services must all be ensured simultaneously for the zone to realise its full potential.

After nearly a decade of delays, the foundation stone of the industrial zone was laid on Monday, formally launching the project. The official implementation period will begin in January next year, with infrastructure construction scheduled for completion by December 2031.

A decade in the making

The economic zone is a joint initiative of the governments of Bangladesh and China. The project was first agreed upon during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Dhaka in 2016.

However, disagreements over the selection of a developer, financing arrangements and contractual terms delayed implementation for years.

Initially, China Harbour Engineering Company was considered as the developer, but the process stalled. In 2022, the Chinese government nominated China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) as the new developer.

During Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to China in June, the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority (BEZA) and CRBC exchanged the developer agreement.

Earlier, on 16 June, the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) approved a Tk 41.89 billion project for supporting infrastructure.

Of the total cost, Tk 17.22 billion will come from the government, and Tk 24.67 billion will be financed through foreign loans.

USD 1.3 billion investment potential

Speaking at the foundation stone-laying ceremony, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said investment in the industrial zone would eventually exceed USD 1 billion, adding that its economic impact would extend beyond Anwara to the whole of southern Chattogram.

Planned infrastructure

The project includes a multipurpose jetty capable of accommodating 20,000-deadweight-ton vessels, a 1,235-metre jetty access road, a bridge, a 1,181-metre, four-lane road, a central effluent treatment plant (CETP) capable of treating 25 million litres of wastewater per day, gas transmission pipelines, two electricity substations, water reservoirs, a solid waste collection centre amd nearly 12 kilometres of boundary wall.

BEZA aims to make at least 60 per cent of the industrial plots factory-ready within the first three years, allowing a significant portion of factories to begin construction by 2030.

A new industrial hub

Since the opening of the Karnaphuli Tunnel, prospects have grown for developing a coastal industrial corridor stretching from Mirsarai through Anwara to Cox's Bazar.

The corridor could integrate ports, industrial zones, power plants, roads and logistics infrastructure into a single economic belt.

Several complementary projects are already underway. The Karnaphuli Tunnel is operational. Construction of the Chinese industrial zone has begun, a project to widen the Anwara–Chandanaish road to four lanes has been approved, a 58-kilometre regional highway from Kalabibir Dighi in Anwara through Banshkhali and Toitong in Pekua to Matamuhuri in Cox's Bazar will also be widened, improving access to Matarbari Deep-Sea Port.

Matarbari Deep-Sea Port is scheduled to begin operations by 2030, while infrastructure for the Chinese economic zone is expected to be completed by 2031. If implemented on schedule, the ports, road network and industrial zone will become fully interconnected.

The industrial zone will also feature its own multipurpose jetty, allowing some raw materials and finished goods to be transported by river, reducing dependence on road transport.

Tunnel usage expected to rise

Before the Karnaphuli Tunnel opened, it was expected to become a major freight route as industrialisation expanded in southern Chattogram and traffic to Matarbari increased.

However, traffic volumes have so far fallen short of expectations.

The tunnel's use is likely to increase once factories in the Chinese industrial zone become operational, as it will be used to transport raw materials and finished products. That increase, however, is not expected immediately, as it will take several years to complete infrastructure, establish factories and begin production.

Infrastructure will determine success

Entrepreneurs say the zone's strategic location has already attracted investor interest, but its long-term success will depend on ensuring uninterrupted supplies of gas, electricity and water, effective waste management and efficient investment services.

They also stress that road projects connecting the zone to Matarbari Port must be completed on time.

Amirul Haque, president of the Chattogram Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told Prothom Alo that the industrial zone's biggest advantage is its proximity to the port. However, he suggested prioritising industries that do not initially require natural gas.

If infrastructure and essential services are delivered on schedule, this industrial zone could become a key hub in the emerging industrial corridor centred on Chattogram Port, the Karnaphuli Tunnel and Matarbari Deep-Sea Port, he said.

item.title: Messi returns as Inter Miami draw 2-2 against Columbus Crew
item.description:
SOCCER-USA/

Lionel Messi returned to Major League Soccer action after World Cup duty on Saturday, coming on in the second half as his Inter Miami side drew 2-2 with Columbus Crew.

Two weeks after Argentina's loss to Spain in the World Cup final, Messi was back on the pitch, entering in the 53rd minute to the delight of fans at Miami's Nu Stadium.

But Messi could not mark his return with a goal, twice shooting wide.

Uruguayan Luis Suarez scored his seventh goal in his last four games to put Miami 1-0 up in the 16th minute.

Messi-less Miami beat Fire 3-2 to spoil Lewandowski's MLS debut

Miami's former Manchester United and Real Madrid midfielder Casemiro scored an own goal in the 34th minute which drew Columbus level at 1-1.

Suarez provided the assist for Noah Allen to head Miami into a 2-1 half-time lead

But midfielder Brais Mendez, making his Columbus debut after arriving from Real Sociedad in Spain, curled in a second equalizer from an 84th-minute free-kick.

The result ended Miami's six-match winning streak and kept them in second place in the Eastern Conference behind Nashville, who drew 2-2 at DC United.

Why did Messi tell his teammates to 'forget everything' before the final?

Los Angeles FC and Vancouver Whitecaps remain level at the top of the Western Conference after they drew 1-1 at Vancouver's BC Place.

Son Heung-min extended his scoring streak since the MLS resumed after the World Cup to four goals in four matches as he put Los Angeles ahead in the 37th minute.

But Vancouver's German star Thomas Mueller converted a 76th-minute penalty.

The former Tottenham star Son, who had shouldered much of the blame for South Korea's failure to make it to the knockout rounds of the World Cup, also earned MVP honors in the MLS All-Star Game on Wednesday.

item.title: Former vice-chancellor's research retracted over misconduct and fraud
item.description:
Former Vice Chancellor of Jashore University of Science and Technology, Professor Md Abdul Majid, has been named among Bangladeshi researchers whose academic papers were retracted by international journals over allegations of plagiarism and research misconduct. He is also a professor in the Department of Pharmaceutical Chemistry at University of Dhaka.

Abdul Majid was appointed the fourth VC of Jashore University of Science and Technology (JUST) on 23 September, 2024. About eight months earlier, in January 2024, two research papers on which he was a co-author were retracted by the academic publisher Hindawi.

One of the retracted studies examined the antioxidant properties of extracts from drumstick (moringa) seeds produced in Bangladesh through scientific and comparative analysis. The other investigated the effectiveness of a cellulose-based nanocomposite in removing harmful substances and protecting biomolecules.

On Saturday, Prothom Alo published a report titled "325 Bangladeshi research papers retracted over plagiarism and irregularities," documenting at least 325 retracted papers between 2019 and June 2026 involving researchers affiliated with Bangladeshi universities and research institutions.

The report has sparked widespread discussion, with many academics and researchers sharing it on social media.

325 Bangladeshi research papers retracted over plagiarism and irregularities

International academic journals typically investigate allegations of misconduct before retracting papers and seek explanations from the authors. However, Abdul Majid told Prothom Alo that he had not been contacted regarding the matter. He said his role in the studies was limited to contributing ideas or conceptual input.

Hindawi''s investigation, however, identified serious irregularities.

According to the publisher, the research data and findings had been generated without conducting the necessary laboratory experiments, and no scientific evidence could be found to support the reliability or validity of the results.

The investigation also concluded that the two papers had been produced or obtained through a "paper mill"—organisations that create, sell, or arrange publication of research papers for a fee.

Hindawi further alleged manipulation of the peer-review process.

According to the investigation, false information was used to mislead the publisher during the independent scientific review process.

DU demotes three teachers for plagiarism

The publisher said it had sought responses from the authors before retracting the papers but found their explanations unsatisfactory.

Since Abdul Majid assumed office as vice-chancellor, multiple research papers affiliated with JUST have also been retracted. Between May 2024 and March 2026, ten papers authored by the university's teachers and students were withdrawn. Another paper was retracted in May this year, bringing the university's total number of retracted papers to 11.

Asked whether he was aware of these incidents, Abdul Majid said, "I had heard about one or two retractions. However, those who faced such issues were not given research awards or involved in other important academic responsibilities."

Researchers with retracted papers also include faculty members from Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology, Jagannath University, Cumilla University, Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University, Bangladesh University of Professionals, Primeasia University, Southeast University, BRAC University and University of Development Alternative, among other public and private universities.

Nadim Mahmud, a researcher at the Department of Neurosciences at University of California San Diego, said plagiarism and research misconduct are regarded as serious ethical violations in Western academia and often result in academic sanctions.

He added that such a culture of accountability has yet to become established in Bangladesh.

item.title: How long your IELTS score is valid? Country-specific rules you should know
item.description:
For anyone planning to study abroad, work overseas or migrate, it is important to know how long an IELTS score remains valid. The IELTS (International English Language Testing System) Test Report Form (TRF), or certificate, has a fixed validity period.

Therefore, alongside preparing for the test itself, candidates should have a clear understanding of how long their score can be used. This is particularly important for students planning to pursue higher education abroad, as an expired score means they must retake the test, reports NDTV.

Under current rules, an IELTS score is valid for two years from the date the results are issued in most countries. The candidate’s Test Report Form (TRF) states both the overall band score and its validity period, along with individual scores for the four components.

Universities where you can study abroad without IELTS

Once the two-year validity period expires, the score is generally no longer accepted for university admission, employment or student visa applications. In such cases, candidates must sit the IELTS test again to obtain a new score.

Rules Vary by Country

Most universities and educational institutions in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and New Zealand do not accept IELTS scores that are more than two years old. Applicants should therefore check in advance whether their score will still be valid when they submit their application.

For those applying for permanent residency in Canada, the IELTS score must also remain valid throughout the application process.

There is no general rule extending IELTS validity to three years for study or employment purposes. However, under certain conditions, some of Australia's skilled migration programmes may accept IELTS scores that are up to three years old.

Same Rule for One Skill Retake?

IELTS now offers the One Skill Retake option. This allows candidates to retake just one of the four test components—Listening, Reading, Writing or Speaking—if they feel their original performance did not accurately reflect their English proficiency.

Candidates who take an IELTS One Skill Retake receive a second Test Report Form, which can be used for study and immigration purposes. The retake must be booked within 60 days of the original IELTS test.

In countries where IELTS One Skill Retake is available, candidates can retake only a single component instead of the entire examination. The updated result is also generally valid for two years.

However, not all universities or immigration authorities accept One Skill Retake results. Candidates should therefore check the relevant institution's policy before choosing this option.

IELTS: Things to do and traps to avoid

Applicants should remember that an IELTS score remains valid for two years from the test date. Anyone planning to study abroad, work overseas, obtain professional registration or migrate should ensure that their score will remain valid throughout the entire application process.

Experts advise students planning to study abroad to schedule their IELTS test in line with university admission deadlines, scholarship applications and visa processing timelines. Doing so helps avoid the risk of the score expiring before the application is completed.

For example, if a student takes the IELTS test on 1 August 2026, the score will generally remain valid until 31 July 2028. After that, a new IELTS test will be required for most fresh applications.
